topics.title: Problem 4 at small error
topics.summary: Which condition on one fixed permutation guarantees worst-start TV at most 2⁻¹²⁸?
body: The brief asks for an explicit round count and allows restricted classes. We compare bounds at 2⁻³², 2⁻⁶⁴ and 2⁻¹²⁸, and ask how the count changes when the target is 2⁻ⁿ.
The leading construction covers four or more inputs and can be checked directly from a compact description. Integer counts on small tables show how rankings can change when the threshold shrinks.
topics.attribution: The project brief supplies the model and allows any positive error target. This research assessment links each construction to its own evidence and priority review.

resources.label: Read the results against the brief
Lower bound from finite key counts

topics.title: A checkable four-input construction
topics.summary: One specified 128-bit permutation certifies triples in 65 rounds and quadruples in 81 rounds at TV 2⁻¹²⁸.
body: XOR a 16-bit projection of a field inverse into the low block, then rotate. Fresh XOR keys translate the arguments of this same update on every round.

The proof bounds parity biases for the translated update and compares two sweeps with independent switch decisions. At error 2⁻ⁿ the construction needs O(t) rounds for all sufficiently large widths and 2 ≤ t ≤ n/2 − 1, choosing the block width for the desired order.
topics.attribution: Niederreiter and Winterhof proved the exact shifted-inverse character estimate in 2000. The round bound for this specified permutation is a project derivation whose publication priority remains unverified.

resources.label: Construction, two-sweep proof and 10-round lower bound

topics.title: Four inputs with a degree-15 update
topics.summary: Any degree-15 control polynomial gives an 89-round guarantee on 128 bits at TV 2⁻¹²⁸ with a 12-bit update.
body: XOR 12 bits of the polynomial output into the low block and rotate. Choosing the fifteenth power gives an update with two field multiplications and three squarings.
A weighted sum of four translates has a surviving coefficient of odd degree. This bounds the correlations among the three relative offsets for a quadruple.
topics.attribution: Makhul and Winterhof give the scalar trace argument. The MiMC paper considers degree 15 for Feistel rounds. The extension to a projected block update and the stated round count are project derivations with unverified priority.

topics.title: Five rounds for a 128-bit seventh power
topics.summary: The field seventh power brings every pair within 2⁻¹²⁸ in at most five rounds, even after up to 2⁶² table changes.
body: All difference rows of a field power follow from one derivative distribution. A multiplicative character bound gives a certificate using only the width and the exponent.
On 128 bits field inversion needs exactly four rounds at error 2⁻¹²⁸. On eight bits that same numerical threshold needs 35 rounds for the inverse and 56 for the seventh power.
topics.attribution: The calculation applies published character-sum bounds and the differential structure of field powers. The small-width hitting times use exact integer convolution.

resources.label: Check a table or a compact power

topics.title: Which field powers mix at every order?
topics.summary: Every nonlinear field power that permutes n-bit strings, n ≥ 3, mixes all tuple sizes through 2ⁿ−2.
body: Checking whether the reduced exponent is a power of two decides eventual mixing. A uniform finite-time bound covers the nonlinear cases but is numerically loose.
For five-bit cubing the exact 2⁻¹²⁸ hitting times are 66 rounds for triples and 67 for quadruples. At three bits the corresponding times are 129 and 258.
topics.attribution: Stafford classified the group generated by field powers and affine maps. Normality gives the repeated-key-schedule corollary. The higher-order finite-width measurements are project computations.

topics.title: What the smaller threshold reveals
topics.summary: Two families that tie at TV 1/4 take 88 and 129 rounds to mix triples at TV 2⁻¹²⁸.
body: Each family contains 10,752 three-bit permutations. The slower triple family is the same one that mixes pairs fastest.
A signed statistic on ordered triples retains information in the slower family. Exact integer paths and small-matrix identities explain the separation.
topics.attribution: O’Connor already enumerated the three-bit APN permutations. The small-error triple profiles and the signed statistic were computed in this project.

resources.label: Tiny-error times and signed orientation proof

topics.title: The difference walk
topics.summary: A shared random XOR key turns the evolution of two inputs into a walk on their nonzero differences.
body: Fix one public permutation P. Each round applies P(x ⊕ K) with a fresh, independent, uniform key K shared by both inputs. Given the current difference a, the next difference is P(x) ⊕ P(x ⊕ a) for a uniformly random x.

The transition matrix has uniform stationary distribution. A finite walk converges to it from every start exactly when the support graph is connected and aperiodic. For this round convention, one extra cipher round converts a difference-distance bound to the ordered-pair bound.
topics.attribution: Lai, Massey and Murphy established the Markov-chain treatment of differential propagation under independent round keys. Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan study almost t-wise independence of key-alternating ciphers. The notebook specializes this framework to a repeated P and keeps track of the final round.

topics.title: The inverse as a benchmark
topics.summary: The three-bit field inverse gives a mixing curve that can be checked exactly by hand.
body: On the eight-element field, fix zero and invert each nonzero element. After two difference rounds, the starting difference has probability 1/4 and each of the six others has probability 1/8.
Every two additional rounds divide the distance to uniform by eight. This benchmark attains the fastest observed pair-mixing time at all six thresholds in the three-bit census.
topics.attribution: The patched inverse is a published construction. Appendix A of Liu–Tessaro–Vaikuntanathan treats an even bit length and a final XOR key. The eight-element calculation here is a project derivation. Jain et al. study a different target, including four-wise convergence of the inverse walk.

topics.title: The three-bit census
topics.summary: Exactly four in five permutations on eight points mix. The other fifth splits into disconnected and periodic walks.
body: Of the ${threeTotal} possible tables, ${threeMix} mix, ${threeDisconnected} have disconnected difference graphs and ${threePeriodic} cycle through seven classes. The last group can reach every difference, but the round number determines the current class.
At total variation distance 1/4, the fastest mixers need three cipher rounds and the slowest need five. The census uses exact integer counts at six cutoffs from 1/4 to 1/128.
topics.attribution: This is an exhaustive computation from the project. O’Connor enumerated all three-bit tables in 1995 and reported the 10,752 ergodic APN permutations. These are exactly the fastest tables at TV 1/4 here. The full status breakdown and six-threshold profiles are project measurements.

topics.title: Counting four-bit permutations
topics.summary: A structural count gives an exact fraction even though there are over twenty trillion labeled permutations.
body: The exact fraction is 179,759/180,180. A four-bit permutation fails if and only if it is affine or permutes the cosets of a proper nonzero binary subspace. Counting overlaps between these families yields 20,873,902,694,400 mixers.

A fixed parity split is preserved with probability 1/35 at three bits and only 1/6,435 at four bits. This accounts for most of the jump in mixing frequency. Independently, the verifier counts graph partitions up to linear changes of basis.
topics.attribution: The coset-block obstruction is published in Caranti et al. Saarinen exhaustively studies other four-bit S-box properties under input/output equivalences. The disjoint count for repeated-P mixing is a project result whose priority remains unverified.

topics.title: Convergence rates
topics.summary: The four-bit mixing curves show far more variation than the three-bit census.

metric.label: distinct curves through ${fourProfileRounds} rounds in the sample

body: A seeded sample of ${fourTotal} four-bit tables contained ${fourMix} mixers. Of those, ${fourCurves} had distinct sequences of worst-case total variation distances through ${fourProfileRounds} difference rounds.

For the original 10,000 draws at seed 20261118, an exact-arithmetic audit certified at least 7,798 distinct asymptotic factors. A parity that is almost preserved helps explain a smaller concentration of slower curves. The histogram describes the sampled tables.
topics.attribution: The seeded sample, measured profiles, and exact rate-separation audit were produced in this project. Spectral analysis of finite Markov chains is established theory.

topics.title: The five-bit count
topics.summary: Exactly one in about 9,694,845 uniformly sampled five-bit tables fails to mix pairs.
body: There are 27,141,314,518,175,866,661,787,402,240 nonmixers among 32! tables. Of these, 61,931,520 have connected graphs of period 31.
A recurrence counts the overlaps among preserved coset partitions in every dimension. At five bits the classification makes the count complete. At six bits some primitive permutations fail as well.
topics.attribution: The coset obstruction and the degree-32 group classification are published. The exact count and recurrence are project derivations with independent checks at three and four bits.

topics.title: The five-bit criterion
topics.summary: At five bits the same two structural obstructions still account for every failure.
body: A preserved coset partition traps differences in a subspace. At degree 32 the primitive-group classification implies that ruling out these partitions forces transitivity on ordered pairs of distinct points.
The remaining possible nontrivial period must divide 31. That forces every difference to have one deterministic successor, so the permutation is affine.
topics.attribution: The coset-block theorem of Caranti et al., the published primitive-group classification recorded in GAP, and the equal sizes of cyclic classes give this dimension-specific corollary.

topics.title: A six-bit counterexample
topics.summary: A nonlinear permutation can preserve no proper subspace partition and still fail to mix.
body: Split six bits into two elements of the eight-element field. Cube both elements and exchange them. An input difference with one nonzero coordinate always has one nonzero coordinate after a round.

Fourteen differences with one active coordinate are separated from the forty-nine with two. The derivative calculation also shows that every invariant binary subspace containing a nonzero difference would have to be the whole space.
topics.attribution: The conserved block weight is a standard product-action observation. The explicit counterexample and verification that it preserves no proper subspace partition are project derivations. Independent priority remains unverified.

topics.title: The orbit criterion
topics.summary: For every bit length, the mixing question can be expressed as a transitivity test on a finite permutation group.
body: Conjugate the XOR translations by every power of P and let H be the group they generate. Pairwise mixing is equivalent to H being transitive on ordered pairs of distinct inputs. The same statement holds on ordered distinct t-tuples.

Group rounds into blocks of length equal to the order of P. Such blocks include the identity and generate H. A block walk converges uniformly on each of its orbits, so one orbit gives the desired uniform law.
topics.attribution: Hornauer, Stephan and Wernsdorf relate periodicity to fixed-length round groups and give a sufficient transitivity condition. The project’s equivalence for the conjugates of translations follows by applying finite-group walk convergence to this key schedule.

topics.title: The three-bit census at every order
topics.summary: On three bits, 80% of permutations mix triples and two thirds mix at every order from four through six.
body: The 5,376 tables that mix triples and fail on quadruples each preserve one relabeling of the fourteen affine planes. An ordered quadruple can detect membership in that family.
The exhaustive calculation gives worst-start hitting times at six TV thresholds. At orders seven and eight, the sign of the composite permutation prevents mixing.
topics.attribution: The exact census and the match to invariant plane systems are project computations. Classical group actions explain the plateau above order four.

topics.title: An exact table test
topics.summary: One graph search returns a decision and a witness for failures.
body: Starting at difference one, generate outgoing XOR differences directly from the table. A proper reached set certifies disconnection. If the search reaches every state, a greatest common divisor of edge-depth discrepancies gives the period.
With N table entries this takes O(N²) worst-case word operations and O(N) words of memory. A native OpenMP version divides rows at a single search depth among workers.
topics.attribution: Denardo published the linear-in-edges period algorithm in 1977. The table-specific transition generator, failure output, and multicore implementation are engineering contributions of this project.

topics.title: A one-sided mixing filter
topics.summary: A randomized table test certifies mixers and bounds the probability of leaving a true mixer unresolved.
body: Every certified table really mixes. For each fixed mixer, the probability of an unresolved result is at most a chosen ε. The proof recovers genuine edges in batches with XOR convolutions and checks that they connect all differences and force period one.

For N = 2ⁿ table entries the worst-case cost is O(N n⁴ log(Nn/ε)) word operations with linear working storage. An optional deterministic fallback gives an exact answer and can still take quadratic time.
topics.attribution: Ahn, Guha and McGregor published graph connectivity sketches using linear measurements. This project adapts sketching, random equality checks, and Walsh transforms to implicit XOR-difference edges and the period test. The exact combination is a candidate contribution with unverified priority.

topics.title: Circuits and black boxes
topics.summary: The cost changes when the permutation is supplied as a short program or an oracle.
body: For n ≥ 3, an exact deterministic oracle test needs 2ⁿ−1 queries in the worst case. Changing two table entries can turn a periodic permutation into a mixer. Allowing a fixed classification error below one half still requires a linear number of queries in the table size.

A different construction encodes a Boolean formula into a compact permutation circuit. The circuit mixes precisely when the formula is satisfiable, proving NP-hardness even when an inverse circuit is supplied.
topics.attribution: The reduction starts from Cook’s published satisfiability theorem. The permutation gadget and the two-entry oracle argument for this decision problem were derived here. Their independent priority remains unverified.

resources.label: Circuit reduction and oracle lower bound

topics.title: Screening for invariant parity
topics.summary: A single binary parity that survives every round certifies disconnection.
body: Look for a nonzero mask m such that m · P(x) and m · x differ by the same constant on every x. The parity of every pairwise difference is then conserved. Binary elimination finds every such mask on a full table.

Sampling a callable yields candidate masks. A union bound controls the chance of retaining a mask that fails on a specified fraction of inputs. A candidate becomes a proof after exhaustive checking or a circuit unsatisfiability certificate.
topics.attribution: This is the hyperplane case of the published coset-block obstruction. The screen implements elementary linear algebra and a sampling bound for this application.

topics.title: What is already known?
topics.summary: Trace the work from differential Markov chains in 1991 to the recent inverse-walk and SPN papers.
body: The review identifies which results use the same public table every round, which model the support as a random graph, and which prove a statement for every starting tuple.
Each research question links to its evidence, including exact counts, finite-round certificates and the remaining proof gaps.
topics.attribution: The cited sources establish the findings attributed to them. Project proofs and measurements have their own entries and priority notes.

topics.title: Three rounds for typical pairs
topics.summary: A typical uniform permutation used in every round mixes every starting pair in exactly three rounds at TV 1/4.
body: After two cipher rounds the worst distance tends to exp(−1/2), about 0.607. After three it tends to zero. The result holds at every fixed threshold strictly between zero and exp(−1/2).
Averaging over a linear relabeling between two copies of the same difference matrix controls the effect of reusing one table. Seeded samples through nine bits accompany the proof.
topics.attribution: O’Connor obtained the one-step law, and O’Connor–Golić studied eventual convergence using a random-graph assumption. The finite-round worst-start proof is a project derivation with unverified priority.

topics.title: Why one parity dominates failure
topics.summary: At large bit lengths, almost every nonmixing permutation preserves a binary parity split.
body: For N = 2ⁿ the failure probability is asymptotic to 2(N−1) / binomial(N,N/2), uniformly for tuple orders 2 through N−2. The number of candidate splits grows only linearly in N, while the probability of preserving one falls exponentially.
The proof counts overlaps among splits and bounds all other block systems and exceptional primitive groups.
topics.attribution: Babai–Hayes already gives qualitative typical generation. The leading equivalent and its attribution to one parity obstruction are derived here from published group bounds.

topics.title: Decide every tuple order
topics.summary: A stabilizer chain determines the highest order that mixes, without enumerating ordered tuples.
body: For n ≥ 3, four-wise mixing is equivalent to the translations and P generating a group containing the alternating group. It gives all orders through N−2.
The solver classified the 10,000 sampled four-bit tables. All 9,974 pair mixers in the sample passed through order 14. The proof supplies a four-bit table the sample missed that stops at three.
topics.attribution: The proof applies published group classification and group algorithms. Explicit examples and sample measurements are supplied by the project.

topics.title: Certify finite pairwise round counts
topics.summary: Quadratic APN tables admit an explicit error bound from a derivative rank test.
body: Test the degree and derivative ranks in O(N n²) word operations. For a certified table, the worst pairwise TV is at most ½√((N−2)/N^(r−1)) after r rounds.
The proof computes the lengths of rows and their overlaps. A weaker bound from row and column support applies even to nonquadratic APN permutations.
topics.attribution: O’Connor used this Gram matrix and gave a three-bit example. The all-width specialization draws on the published hyperplane geometry of crooked functions.

resources.label: Rank test and exact chi-squared distance

topics.title: A three-round certificate for triples
topics.summary: If a table differs from field inversion at h entries, every starting triple is within (7+6h)/N of uniform after three rounds.
body: For the inverse on five bits the bound is 7/32, already below 1/4. At eight bits up to nine table changes still fit the same threshold.
Projective linear maps act sharply transitively on ordered triples. Counting the maps realized by three translations and coupling back to finite field inversion gives the guarantee.
topics.attribution: The proof combines classical projective geometry with the published inverse-walk approximation. For the exact inverse the three-round distance is 7/N + O(1/N²) for every start. Priority of the explicit finite bound and perturbation certificate is unverified.

topics.title: The three-round triple distance
topics.summary: At seven bits the sampled median TV for one starting triple drops from 0.3745 after three rounds to 0.0372 after four.
body: The experiment measures exact distances for (0,1,2) on 32 random tables per bit length, from four through seven bits.
Four rounds are optimal at TV 1/4. After three rounds the distance is between 1/3 and 1/2 up to vanishing error with high probability. Does it converge to exp(−1)?
topics.attribution: The values are project measurements. The limiting three-round distance for a typical table remains open.

topics.title: Four rounds for typical triples
topics.summary: At TV 1/4, a uniformly sampled table reused each round typically needs exactly four cipher rounds to mix triples.
body: Compare two independent key paths that start at the same triple and share the same table. The chance their final shapes agree is N⁻² + O(N⁻³). This controls total variation distance for one start. Concentration over the random table makes the bound simultaneous over all starts.

A second finite calculation proves three rounds typically leave at least 1/3 minus a vanishing error in TV. The two bounds give the exact typical round count at every fixed threshold below 1/3. Independent enumerations check the computer-assisted steps.
topics.attribution: Computer-assisted project proof. The result concerns one unrestricted uniform public table reused across rounds. Publication priority remains unverified.

resources.label: Three-round lower bound and exact mixing time

topics.title: The exact six-bit fraction
topics.summary: The recurrence counts all preserved coset partitions. Which other six-bit permutations fail, and how many are there?
body: Primitive groups can still fail to mix pairs at six bits, as the explicit two-coordinate example shows. A complete count must handle these cases and avoid double-counting permutations with several descriptions.
topics.attribution: The six-bit gap concerns the exact finite count. The leading asymptotic and the count for every imprimitive table are available.

topics.title: How many rounds for four inputs?
topics.summary: Typical tables need three rounds for pairs and four for triples at TV 1/4. Does a similar rule hold for quadruples?
body: Ordered quadruples on binary vectors can form an affine plane or be affinely independent. A worst-start result must cover both kinds.

The field inverse already shows that fast triple mixing can coexist with very slow quadruple mixing. The open question here concerns the round count for a typical uniform fixed table. The small-error branch gives a separate explicit family with a four-input certificate.
topics.attribution: The inverse lower bound is published. The typical random-table round count for quadruples remains open.
